opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the fact that the workloads have changed so fundamentally. For decades, most of the software stack was designed around a fairly predictable model: you have CPUs, you have applications that are mostly about processing data or serving web requests, and the scaling challenges, while hard, were well understood. We built databases, distributed file systems, big data frameworks like Hadoop and later Spark, all around that world.

With AI, a few things happened at once. First, the hardware changed. Now it's GPUs and other accelerators, and they're extremely expensive, so utilization matters enormously. If you leave a GPU idle, you're burning a lot of money. Second, the workloads are much more heterogeneous. A single AI application might involve data preprocessing on CPUs, training on thousands of GPUs, then fine-tuning, evaluation, and serving with very different latency and throughput requirements. And increasingly, with reinforcement learning and agents, these phases are tightly interleaved rather than being separate pipelines.

Third, the scale is unprecedented. The demand for compute has been growing far faster than Moore's law ever delivered, which means you simply can't run these workloads on a single machine. Everything becomes a distributed systems problem. And distributed systems are hard: you have to deal with failures, scheduling, data movement, and memory management across many nodes.

So when you look at each layer, from the cluster manager, to the scheduler, to the distributed execution framework, to the inference engine, to how you manage the KV cache, many of the assumptions baked into the existing systems just don't hold anymore. That's why we saw the need for things like Ray, to provide a general-purpose way to scale Python and AI workloads, and later vLLM, because serving large language models efficiently required rethinking memory management in a way that borrowed ideas from operating systems, like paging.

In some sense, it's a very exciting time to be a systems researcher. It's rare that you get an opportunity where almost every layer of the stack needs to be revisited. The last time we saw something comparable was probably the shift to the cloud and big data, and I think this one is even bigger.

r001.rationale: It says AI compute demand has outgrown what a single machine can run and that workloads require distributed systems, after describing GPUs and other accelerators.

r002.rationale: It mentions GPUs and other accelerators and separately describes heterogeneous workloads, but does not identify accelerator proliferation as a source of that heterogeneity.

r003.rationale: It says Ray helps scale Python and AI workloads, but does not state that the stack should hide distributed infrastructure complexity from application developers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the assumptions the existing stack was built on don't hold anymore. Most of our systems, from operating systems to databases to the cloud itself, were designed around workloads that are fairly predictable, run on commodity CPUs, and where the scarce resource is something like I/O or memory bandwidth. AI workloads break almost every one of those assumptions at once.

Take the hardware. We've moved from a world where you had one kind of processor and a fairly uniform machine to a world of GPUs, TPUs, custom accelerators, with very different memory hierarchies and very different interconnects. The accelerator is now the expensive, scarce resource, and it sits idle a surprising amount of the time because the rest of the stack, the scheduler, the data loading, the networking, wasn't designed to keep it fed. So you end up rethinking scheduling, you rethink how data moves, you rethink what a "node" even means.

Then there's the workload itself. Training a large model is a tightly coupled distributed computation that looks nothing like a web request or a MapReduce job. You have thousands of accelerators that need to stay in lockstep, failures are frequent at that scale, and the state you need to checkpoint is enormous. Classic fault tolerance, where you just retry a task, doesn't map cleanly onto that. And inference is a different animal again. It's latency sensitive, the compute per request is wildly variable depending on how long the output is, and memory for things like the KV cache becomes the bottleneck. So you need new abstractions for serving, for batching, for managing memory, which is really what motivated systems like vLLM.

And there's the programming model layer. Building an AI application today means stitching together training, data processing, serving, maybe reinforcement learning, maybe agents that call tools and other models. These used to be separate systems with separate teams. Increasingly you need them to compose in one pipeline, and ideally in a language like Python that the people building the models actually use. That's a lot of what we were going after with Ray, giving people a general distributed substrate so they don't have to glue five different frameworks together.

Finally, the economics are different. Compute is now the dominant cost, not engineers, which flips a lot of the optimization trade-offs we've gotten used to. When a cluster costs what it does today, a ten percent utilization improvement is a very big deal, and that pushes you to reconsider layers of the stack you'd normally never touch.

So it's not that any single layer is wrong. It's that the hardware, the workload, the programming model, and the economics all shifted at the same time, and when that happens you don't get to just patch the old stack. You have to go back to first principles.

r001.rationale: The response describes large-scale, tightly coupled training across thousands of accelerators, but does not state that AI application demands are outgrowing the capacity of a single node, even with accelerators.

r002.rationale: It names GPUs, TPUs, and custom accelerators and explains that their differing memory hierarchies and interconnects make the hardware heterogeneous.

r003.rationale: It presents Ray as a general distributed substrate that avoids gluing frameworks together, but does not clearly say the stack should hide distributed, heterogeneous infrastructure complexity from application developers.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the main reason is that AI changes the workload and, with it, the assumptions behind the software stack. In traditional software, you write the logic explicitly. With AI, you learn much of that logic from data. So managing the data, training the model, and serving the model become central parts of building an application.

And the computational requirements are very different. You have accelerators, you have computations distributed across many machines, and you need to move data efficiently between them. It’s not enough to have a fast GPU. If the GPU is waiting for data or for another GPU, you’re wasting a very expensive resource. That forces you to rethink scheduling, storage, networking, and execution together.

At the application level, you also have a different challenge: the output is probabilistic. How do you test it? How do you monitor quality? How do you trade off quality against latency and cost? Those questions affect the abstractions developers need.

So it’s not that every piece of existing software disappears. It’s that the workload has changed enough that we need to revisit the decisions we made at almost every layer.

r001.rationale: The response mentions accelerators and computation distributed across many machines, but does not say AI demands are growing beyond what a single node can handle.

r002.rationale: It mentions accelerators, but does not identify a proliferation of different accelerator types or increasing hardware heterogeneity.

r003.rationale: It says infrastructure decisions and developer abstractions need rethinking, but does not state that the stack should hide distributed, heterogeneous infrastructure complexity from application developers.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, AI changes the workload, and that changes the assumptions behind the stack. In traditional software, you write the program that specifies the behavior. With AI, you use data and computation to learn that behavior. So managing the data, training the model, and serving it become central parts of the application.

And these workloads have very different requirements. Training involves coordinating computation across many accelerators. If you cannot move data efficiently or keep those accelerators busy, you waste very expensive resources. Serving introduces another set of tradeoffs: you want low latency, high throughput, and good model quality, while controlling cost.

These decisions are connected. The model you choose affects memory requirements, scheduling, and how you distribute computation. So you cannot just optimize each layer independently. You have to rethink the interfaces between the layers, and often the layers themselves, around this new workload.

r001.rationale: It says training coordinates computation across many accelerators, but does not state that AI demands are growing faster than a single node's capabilities.

r002.rationale: It mentions many accelerators, but does not identify proliferating accelerators or increasing hardware heterogeneity.

r003.rationale: It calls for rethinking stack layers and interfaces, but does not say the stack should hide distributed, heterogeneous infrastructure complexity from application developers.
